reference.source: Hand surgery and sports medicine references
clinicalPearls: An often-missed fracture presenting with ulnar-sided, hypothenar wrist pain, typically in racquet, bat or club sports
The mechanism is usually a direct blow to the hypothenar area, such as from the butt of a club or bat, or a fall
Tenderness is localised over the hook of the hamate, and grip may be painful and weak
It is frequently missed on standard radiographs, and CT is the most reliable imaging
Nearby structures are at risk, including the ulnar nerve and artery and the flexor tendons of the little finger
Nonunion is common, and symptomatic cases are often treated by excision of the fractured hook
reference.pathophysiology: The hook of the hamate projects into the palm and forms part of the ulnar carpal tunnel (Guyon canal) and the origin of hypothenar muscles. A direct blow or repetitive impact fractures the hook, and because it has a relatively tenuous blood supply and is subject to shear from attached ligaments and tendons, healing is often poor, leading to nonunion. Its proximity to the ulnar nerve and artery and to the flexor tendons explains the associated neurovascular symptoms and the risk of attritional tendon rupture.
additionalDifferentials: Guyon canal syndrome of other cause
additionalInvestigations: CT of the wrist, the most sensitive test for the fracture
Dedicated carpal tunnel or oblique radiographic views
Assessment of ulnar nerve and artery function
Evaluation of the little and ring finger flexor tendons
MRI where soft-tissue or vascular injury is suspected
redFlags: Little or ring finger flexor tendon rupture
Persistent pain from an established nonunion
Missed diagnosis with ongoing grip weakness
reference.prognosis: With diagnosis and appropriate treatment, including excision of a symptomatic nonunited hook, outcomes are generally good, whereas missed fractures can cause chronic pain, nerve symptoms and tendon rupture.
pitfalls: Relying on standard radiographs and missing the fracture
Overlooking ulnar nerve or artery involvement
Failing to recognise attritional flexor tendon rupture
Attributing persistent ulnar wrist pain to a simple sprain
